text: AI is running out of internet. The next wave of models, especially robots, needs real first-person data: what a person actually sees and hears. Right now that data is either scraped without consent or locked inside a few big labs. Labs can't tell real data from synthetic fakes, and the people who capture it never get paid. This is Odyssey.

These are our capture glasses: an E S P thirty-two camera, a microphone and a small transparent display, with a private key that never leaves the device. When you capture, the glasses hash the clip and sign it right at the sensor, before it ever touches a server. Our gateway checks the signature, encrypts the payload, and stores it.

The easiest way to cheat a data network is to run a thousand fake devices, so every pair of glasses is tied to one real person. You enter the glasses' address and prove you're human with World I D. It reveals nothing about who you are, and the proof is bound to that exact device address, so it can't be reused. One human, one device. This screen is a demo; the live page runs the same two steps.

Every sample carries its own proof: which device took it, when and where, a content hash and the device's signature. And this one is real: a photo our glasses uploaded today, stored as an entity on Archive. Anyone can see the device address, the World I D that captured it, the location and the signature. The photo itself is encrypted, so only someone who paid can read it. Proof is public; data stays private.

Now the buyer's side. An AI lab picks an area and a kind of data, and subscribes for thirty days, paid in zero G. Once subscribed, it gets a live map of every hexagon its data covers and how validators scored each one. Payments go through our subscriptions contract on zero G Galileo; here it is, with a real subscription payment on-chain. Seventy percent of every payment is set aside for the people who captured the data, and only the rest goes to the platform.

Labs don't even have to download anything to explore. Our hosted M C P server lets Claude, Cursor or any M C P client search the data a wallet has paid for, with three tools: list datasets, search samples, get a sample.

Checking every sample doesn't scale, so validators spot-check a small share, and only objective evidence counts. If someone re-uploads another person's clip, that's provable: a strike. Two strikes and that World I D is banned: no uploads, no new devices, and their data can't be decrypted. Bans live on our consensus contract on zero G, here with the validator votes and the bans we tested.

Contributors see what they earned each reward epoch and claim it straight from the contract with a Merkle proof. Odyssey: real-world data, signed at the sensor, owned by the people who capture it. Everything you saw is open source, with links below.
